items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "nutrition"?
options: The taking in of materials for energy, growth and development.
The chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules and release energy for metabolism.
The ability to detect and respond to changes in the internal or external environment.
An action by an organism or part of an organism causing a change of position or place.
items.answer: The taking in of materials for energy, growth and development.
items.markingKey: Nutrition: the taking in of materials for energy, growth and development.

items.stem: Which term is defined as "the processes that make more of the same kind of organism"?
items.answer: Reproduction
items.markingKey: Reproduction: the processes that make more of the same kind of organism.

items.stem: A car moves, uses fuel and oxygen, and releases carbon dioxide and water. Explain why a car is not a living organism.
items.answer: It does not show all seven characteristics: it cannot grow, reproduce or respond (sensitivity) on its own, and its "fuel use" is combustion, not respiration in cells.
items.markingKey: must show all seven characteristics [1]; cannot grow / reproduce / be sensitive [1]; no cells / combustion is not respiration [1] [3]

items.stem: Name the characteristic of living organisms shown by each example. (i) A strawberry plant producing runners that form new plants. (ii) Chloroplasts moving around inside a leaf cell.
items.answer: (i) reproduction (ii) movement
items.markingKey: (i) reproduction [1]; (ii) movement [1] [2]

items.stem: Arjun, a student in Nairobi, investigates a jelly-like blob found on a forest log. Observations: it creeps slowly across the log; it engulfs bacteria; it moves away from bright light. (a) List the characteristics of living organisms suggested by these observations. (b) Name two other characteristics that must be tested before concluding that it is alive, and suggest how one could be tested.
items.answer: (a) movement, nutrition, sensitivity. (b) respiration and growth; e.g. test for carbon dioxide release or oxygen uptake (e.g. hydrogencarbonate indicator).
items.markingKey: (a) movement, nutrition, sensitivity (all correct) [2] (b) two characteristics not yet observed [1]; valid test [1] [2]

items.stem: Which list contains only characteristics shared by all living organisms?
items.answer: excretion, growth, nutrition
items.markingKey: All seven (movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition) are shown by every living organism.

items.stem: Elena grew bean seedlings in Hanoi. A sample of seedlings had a fresh mass of 8.1 g and a dry mass of 0.8 g at the start. After 7 days a similar sample had a fresh mass of 14.5 g and a dry mass of 1.6 g. Calculate the percentage increase in dry mass.

Name the characteristic of living organisms shown by each example. (i) A plant absorbing nitrate ions from the soil. (ii) Urea being removed from the body in urine. (iii) The pupils of a cat narrowing in bright light. (iv) A caterpillar eating a leaf.
items.answer: (i) nutrition (ii) excretion (iii) sensitivity (iv) nutrition
items.markingKey: (i) nutrition [1]; (ii) excretion [1]; (iii) sensitivity [1]; (iv) nutrition [1] [4]

items.stem: Ravi, a student in Lima, investigates a robot vacuum cleaner. Observations: it moves around a room; it changes direction when it touches a wall; it takes in electrical energy from a charger. (a) List the characteristics of living organisms suggested by these observations. (b) Explain why seeing an increase in size alone is not enough evidence of growth in a living organism.
items.answer: (a) movement, sensitivity, nutrition. (b) Increase in size could be temporary (e.g. water uptake) or non-living accumulation; growth must be a permanent increase in dry mass.
items.markingKey: (a) movement, sensitivity, nutrition (all correct) [2] (b) temporary / non-living increase possible [1]; permanent increase in dry mass needed [1] [2]

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "the offspring of two different species, which is usually infertile"?
items.answer: Hybrid
items.markingKey: Hybrid: the offspring of two different species, which is usually infertile.

items.stem: Explain why classification systems group organisms using shared features.
items.answer: Organisms that share many features are likely to be closely related (share a recent common ancestor), so grouping by shared features reflects evolutionary relationships and makes organisms easier to identify and study.
items.markingKey: shared features suggest relationship / common ancestry [1]; useful for identification / prediction [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a dichotomous key uses visible features rather than features such as diet or behaviour.
items.answer: Visible features can be checked directly on the specimen at any time, so different people get the same result; diet or behaviour may not be observable.
items.markingKey: features observable on specimen [1]; reliable / consistent identification [1] [2]

items.stem: A student uses this dichotomous key to identify leaf-litter invertebrates. Key: 1a has legs ... go to 2; 1b has no legs ... snail | 2a has six legs ... go to 3; 2b does not have six legs ... millipede | 3a has wings ... beetle; 3b has no wings ... ant. The specimen has these features: has six legs; has legs; does not have eight legs; has no wings. Use the key to identify the specimen.
items.answer: ant
items.markingKey: ant: follow each pair of statements in turn [1]

items.stem: A student uses this dichotomous key to identify leaves from trees in a park. Key: 1a leaf is divided into leaflets ... ash; 1b leaf is a single blade ... go to 2 | 2a leaf edge has spines ... holly; 2b leaf edge has no spines ... go to 3 | 3a leaf edge has rounded or pointed lobes ... maple; 3b leaf edge has no lobes ... go to 4 | 4a leaf edge is finely toothed ... birch; 4b leaf edge is smooth ... beech. The specimen has these features: leaf is divided into leaflets; leaflets arranged in pairs along a central stalk. (a) Use the key to identify the specimen. (b) State the features that the key gives for the holly.
items.answer: (a) ash (b) leaf is a single blade; leaf edge has spines
items.markingKey: (a) ash [1] (b) features from the key: leaf is a single blade; leaf edge has spines [2]

items.stem: Aisha collects leaves from trees in a park on a field trip near Auckland. Their features are: holly: leaf is a single blade, leaf edge has spines; ash: leaf is divided into leaflets, leaflets arranged in pairs along a central stalk; oak: leaf is a single blade, leaf edge has no spines, leaf edge has rounded or pointed lobes; beech: leaf is a single blade, leaf edge has no spines, leaf edge has no lobes, leaf edge is smooth; birch: leaf is a single blade, leaf edge has no spines, leaf edge has no lobes, leaf edge is finely toothed. (a) Explain why the key must use features that do not change during the life of the organism or with the season. (b) Suggest one other method, apart from a key, that could be used to check the identification of an organism.
items.answer: (a) Otherwise the same species could be identified differently at different times (e.g. juveniles or seasonal changes). (b) Compare its DNA base sequences with known species (or compare with a labelled reference specimen / field guide photograph).
items.markingKey: (a) features must be constant [1]; reliable identification [1] [2] (b) DNA sequencing / reference collection [1]

items.stem: Which is the correct way to write the scientific name of the lion?
options: panthera leo (both words in lower case)
Panthera leo (genus capitalised, species in lower case, in italics)
items.answer: Panthera leo (genus capitalised, species in lower case, in italics)
items.markingKey: Genus with a capital letter, species with a lower-case letter, both in italics (or underlined when handwritten).

items.stem: Explain why each step of a dichotomous key has exactly two statements.
items.answer: Dichotomous means dividing in two: each pair of opposite statements splits the group into two smaller groups until each organism is identified.
items.markingKey: two contrasting statements [1]; group divided until one organism remains [1] [2]

items.stem: Panthera tigris and Panthera onca share a genus but Canis lupus does not. Explain what this suggests about their relationships.
items.answer: The two Panthera species are more closely related to each other (share a more recent common ancestor) than either is to Canis lupus.
items.markingKey: same genus = closely related [1]; more recent common ancestor [1] [2]

items.stem: Three organisms have the scientific names Equus zebra, Homo sapiens and Equus caballus. (a) State which two are most closely related and give a reason.
items.answer: (a) Equus zebra and Equus caballus: they share the genus Equus.
items.markingKey: (a) Equus zebra and Equus caballus [1]; same genus (Equus) [1] [2]

items.stem: Three organisms have the scientific names Felis catus, Panthera tigris and Panthera pardus. (a) State which two are most closely related and give a reason. (b) State the genus of the third organism.
items.answer: (a) Panthera pardus and Panthera tigris: they share the genus Panthera. (b) Felis
items.markingKey: (a) Panthera pardus and Panthera tigris [1]; same genus (Panthera) [1] (b) Felis [1] [3]

items.stem: Hana collects leaves from trees in a park on a field trip near Auckland. Their features are: horse chestnut: leaf is divided into leaflets, leaflets spread out from one point; ash: leaf is divided into leaflets, leaflets arranged in pairs along a central stalk; maple: leaf is a single blade, leaf edge has no spines, leaf edge has rounded or pointed lobes, lobes are pointed; holly: leaf is a single blade, leaf edge has spines; birch: leaf is a single blade, leaf edge has no spines, leaf edge has no lobes, leaf edge is finely toothed. (a) Construct a dichotomous key to identify these organisms. (b) Suggest one other method, apart from a key, that could be used to check the identification of an organism.
items.answer: (a) 1a leaf is divided into leaflets ... go to 2; 1b leaf is a single blade ... go to 3 | 2a leaflets spread out from one point ... horse chestnut; 2b leaflets arranged in pairs along a central stalk ... ash | 3a leaf edge has spines ... holly; 3b leaf edge has no spines ... go to 4 | 4a leaf edge has rounded or pointed lobes ... maple; 4b leaf edge has no lobes ... birch (b) Compare its DNA base sequences with known species (or compare with a labelled reference specimen / field guide photograph).
items.markingKey: (a) paired contrasting statements at each step [1]; each organism reached at a separate end-point [1]; uses features given, not size or colour [1]; 4 steps [1] [4] (b) DNA sequencing / reference collection [1]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "fern"?
options: A plant with roots, stems and fronds that reproduces by spores, not seeds.
A flowering plant with two seed leaves, branching leaf veins and flower parts in fours or fives.
An animal with a backbone (vertebral column).
A flowering plant with one seed leaf, parallel leaf veins and flower parts in threes.
items.answer: A plant with roots, stems and fronds that reproduces by spores, not seeds.
items.markingKey: Fern: a plant with roots, stems and fronds that reproduces by spores, not seeds.

items.stem: Explain why a whale is classified as a mammal and not as a fish.
items.answer: It has mammal features: hair (a few bristles), mammary glands producing milk, lungs breathing air, and the young develop in the uterus with a placenta; fish have gills and wet scales.
items.markingKey: two mammal features [2]; lacks fish features (gills / scales) [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why a bat is not a bird even though it can fly.
items.answer: It has fur, external ears, gives birth to live young and feeds them milk, which are mammal features; it has no feathers or beak.
items.markingKey: mammal features named [1]; no feathers / beak [1] [2]

items.stem: A specimen found near Auckland has these features: wet scales on the skin; fins. To which group does it belong?
items.answer: fish
items.markingKey: Fish: wet scales on the skin; gills for gas exchange; fins; a lateral line.

items.stem: A specimen found near Lagos has these features: young that develop inside the mother, attached by a placenta; four limbs and a diaphragm; mammary glands producing milk. (a) Name the group it belongs to. (b) Give one feature that would distinguish it from reptiles. (c) Name one other organism in the same group.
items.answer: (a) mammals (b) e.g. fur or hair on the skin (not found in reptiles) (c) e.g. bat
items.markingKey: (a) mammals [1] (b) a feature of mammals absent in reptiles, e.g. fur or hair on the skin [1] (c) correct example such as bat [1] [3]

items.stem: On a field trip in Bogotá, Zara finds two animals. Animal P has three pairs of jointed legs and two pairs of wings in most species. Animal Q has one or two pairs of legs on each segment and a body not divided into thorax and abdomen. (a) Name the group to which each animal belongs. (b) Explain why classifying organisms into groups is useful to scientists.
items.answer: (a) P: insects; Q: myriapods (b) It shows how organisms are related (common ancestry), makes identification easier and allows predictions about features of newly found organisms.
items.markingKey: (a) P insects [1]; Q myriapods [1] [2] (b) relationships / evolution [1]; identification or prediction [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why amphibians must return to water to reproduce.
items.answer: Their eggs have no shell and would dry out on land, and the larvae (tadpoles) have gills and live in water.
items.markingKey: eggs lack shells / would dry out [1]; larvae aquatic with gills [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how the eggs of reptiles and birds are adapted to development on land.
items.answer: They have a shell (leathery or hard) that reduces water loss and protects the embryo, so they need not be laid in water.
items.markingKey: shell present [1]; prevents drying / protects embryo [1] [2]

items.stem: A specimen found near Jakarta has these features: a body in three parts: head, thorax and abdomen; three pairs of jointed legs. To which group does it belong?
items.answer: insects
items.markingKey: Insects: three pairs of jointed legs; a body in three parts: head, thorax and abdomen; one pair of antennae; two pairs of wings in most species.

items.stem: An animal found near Nairobi has these features: no wings; a body in two parts: cephalothorax and abdomen. To which group does it belong?
items.answer: arachnids
items.markingKey: Arachnids: four pairs of jointed legs; a body in two parts: cephalothorax and abdomen; no antennae; no wings.

items.stem: A plant found near Lisbon has these features: flower parts in multiples of three; one cotyledon in the seed; leaves with parallel veins. (a) Name the group it belongs to. (b) Give one feature that would distinguish it from ferns. (c) Name one other organism in the same group.
items.answer: (a) monocotyledons (b) e.g. one cotyledon in the seed (not found in ferns) (c) e.g. rice
items.markingKey: (a) monocotyledons [1] (b) a feature of monocotyledons absent in ferns, e.g. one cotyledon in the seed [1] (c) correct example such as rice [1] [3]

items.stem: On a field trip in Riyadh, Kenji finds two animals. Animal P has many body segments and a body not divided into thorax and abdomen. Animal Q has two pairs of wings in most species and three pairs of jointed legs. (a) Name the group to which each animal belongs. (b) State one feature shared by both animals that places them in the same larger group. (c) Suggest why a scientist might check the classification of animal Q by comparing DNA as well as visible features.
items.answer: (a) P: myriapods; Q: insects (b) Jointed legs / exoskeleton / segmented body (arthropods). (c) Visible features may be similar because of similar environments (not relationship); DNA base sequences show how closely related organisms are more accurately.
items.markingKey: (a) P myriapods [1]; Q insects [1] [2] (b) [1] (c) features can mislead (convergence) [1]; DNA similarity = relatedness [1] [2]

items.stem: Which term is defined as "a non-cellular particle made of genetic material surrounded by a protein coat"?
items.answer: Virus
items.markingKey: Virus: a non-cellular particle made of genetic material surrounded by a protein coat.

items.stem: Explain why DNA base sequences are used to classify organisms.
items.answer: Closely related species share a recent common ancestor, so their DNA base sequences are more similar; the number of differences shows how closely related they are and can correct mistakes from visible features.
items.markingKey: related organisms have similar sequences [1]; fewer differences = more recent common ancestor [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why fungi were moved out of the plant kingdom.
items.answer: Fungi have no chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesise, have cell walls of chitin not cellulose, and feed by extracellular digestion; DNA evidence shows they are a separate group.
items.markingKey: two differences from plants [2]

items.stem: Part of the same gene was sequenced in four species. Species A: CTCGAACCTTGT; species D: CTCGAACGTTGT; species E: CTGGGACGCTAT; species C: CTCGAACCTTTC. Identify the species most closely related to species A. Show your working.
items.answer: Differences from A: D 1, E 5, C 2. Species D is most closely related.
items.markingKey: counts differences correctly [1]; species D (fewest differences) [1] [2]

items.stem: Part of the same gene was sequenced in four species. Species A: CAGTTTTGATGTATTA; species C: CAGTTTTGATGTAATA; species D: CAGTATTGATGTCATA; species B: CAGTTTTGACGTTTTA. (a) Identify the species most closely related to A, showing your working. (b) Calculate the percentage of bases in species C that are the same as in species A.
items.answer: (a) Differences from A: C 1, D 3, B 2. Species C is most closely related. (b) 93.8%
items.markingKey: (a) counts differences correctly [1]; species C (fewest differences) [1] (b) (16 − 1) ÷ 16 × 100 = 93.8% [1] [3]

items.stem: Freya compares a 200-base section of DNA from three frog species, X, Y and Z, found in different valleys near Nairobi. Y and X differ at 7 bases; Z and X differ at 26 bases; Z and Y differ at 2 bases. Z and X look very similar; Y looks different. (a) State which two species are most closely related. Explain your answer. (b) Suggest why Z and X look similar even though they are less closely related.
items.answer: (a) Z and Y: fewest base differences (2). (b) They live in similar habitats, so similar features were selected (convergence); appearance does not always show relationship.
items.markingKey: (a) Z and Y [1]; fewest differences / most similar sequence [1] [2] (b) similar environment / selection pressures [1]; visible features not reliable [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why viruses are described as being on the boundary of living and non-living.
items.answer: They contain genetic material and reproduce, but only inside a host cell; outside cells they show no respiration, nutrition, excretion or growth.
items.markingKey: reproduce only in host cells [1]; do not show other characteristics on their own [1] [2]

items.stem: Compare the structure of a prokaryotic cell and a cell from the plant kingdom.
items.answer: Both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, cell wall and ribosomes. Prokaryote: no nucleus (circular DNA, plasmids), no chloroplasts or mitochondria, wall not cellulose. Plant: nucleus, chloroplasts, mitochondria, cellulose wall, vacuole.
items.markingKey: one similarity [1]; two differences [2] [3]

items.stem: An organism has these features: nucleus present; mostly single-celled; some have chloroplasts, some feed like animals. Name the kingdom and state one feature that distinguishes it from prokaryotes.
items.answer: Protoctists; e.g. nucleus present.
items.markingKey: protoctists [1]; a valid distinguishing feature [1] [2]

items.stem: Part of the same gene was sequenced in four species. Species A: ATCCGTGTGGCCCAGG; species B: ATCCTTGTCGCACAGG; species E: ATCAGTGTGGCCCAGG; species D: TTCCCTGTGACATAGG. (a) Identify the species most closely related to A, showing your working. (b) Calculate the percentage of bases in species E that are the same as in species A. (c) Explain why comparing DNA is more reliable than comparing visible features.
items.answer: (a) Differences from A: B 3, E 1, D 5. Species E is most closely related. (b) 93.8% (c) DNA differences reflect how recently species shared a common ancestor; visible features can be similar for other reasons.
items.markingKey: (a) counts differences correctly [1]; species E (fewest differences) [1] (b) (16 − 1) ÷ 16 × 100 = 93.8% [1] (c) DNA reflects common ancestry / features can evolve similarly in similar habitats [1] [4]

items.stem: Describe the main features of the five kingdoms of living organisms.
items.answer: Animals: multicellular, no walls, nervous coordination, heterotrophic. Plants: multicellular, cellulose walls, chloroplasts. Fungi: hyphae, chitin walls, saprotrophic. Protoctists: mostly single-celled with nucleus. Prokaryotes: no nucleus, circular DNA, plasmids.
items.markingKey: one correct distinguishing feature for each of five kingdoms [5]

items.stem: Ines compares a 200-base section of DNA from three bird species, X, Y and Z, found in different valleys near Nairobi. Y and X differ at 16 bases; Z and X differ at 27 bases; Z and Y differ at 10 bases. Z and X look very similar; Y looks different. (a) State which two species are most closely related. Explain your answer. (b) Calculate the percentage difference between the DNA of Z and X. (c) Suggest why Z and X look similar even though they are less closely related.
items.answer: (a) Z and Y: fewest base differences (10). (b) 13.5% (c) They live in similar habitats, so similar features were selected (convergence); appearance does not always show relationship.
items.markingKey: (a) Z and Y [1]; fewest differences / most similar sequence [1] [2] (b) 27 ÷ 200 × 100 [1] = 13.5% [1] [2] (c) similar environment / selection pressures [1]; visible features not reliable [1] [2]

items.stem: Which process releases energy from nutrient molecules in all living cells?
items.answer: Respiration
items.markingKey: Respiration is the chemical breakdown of nutrient molecules in cells to release energy; breathing is only the movement of air.

items.stem: Explain why scientists measure dry mass, not fresh mass, when measuring the growth of a plant.
items.answer: Fresh mass changes with the amount of water the plant has taken up or lost; dry mass measures the permanent increase in organic material.
items.markingKey: water content varies / is temporary [1]; dry mass shows permanent increase in biomass [1] [2]

items.stem: Name the characteristic of living organisms shown by each example. (i) A frog laying fertilised eggs. (ii) An owl turning its head towards a rustling sound.
items.answer: (i) reproduction (ii) sensitivity
items.markingKey: (i) reproduction [1]; (ii) sensitivity [1] [2]

items.stem: Mohammed, a student in Bangkok, investigates an unknown green film growing on a pond wall. Observations: it gains mass only when light is present; it spreads over the wall each week; oxygen bubbles are released in light. (a) Evaluate whether there is enough evidence to classify it as a living organism. (b) Explain why seeing an increase in size alone is not enough evidence of growth in a living organism.
items.answer: (a) Not yet: only 3 of the seven characteristics are shown; a living organism must show all seven — machines and crystals can show one or two. (b) Increase in size could be temporary (e.g. water uptake) or non-living accumulation; growth must be a permanent increase in dry mass.
items.markingKey: (a) all seven needed [1]; refers to the evidence given [1]; conclusion [1] [3] (b) temporary / non-living increase possible [1]; permanent increase in dry mass needed [1] [2]

items.stem: Felis catus (domestic cat) and Felis silvestris (wildcat) belong to the same
items.answer: genus
items.markingKey: The first part of the binomial name (Felis) is the genus.

items.stem: Suggest why feature such as "large" or "dark" should not be used in a dichotomous key.
items.answer: They are relative / subjective, so different people would make different decisions; key statements should be clear and measurable.
items.markingKey: subjective / depends on comparison [1]; use definite features (e.g. number of legs) [1] [2]

items.stem: A student in Muscat states: "A dichotomous key can use three choices at each step." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: A dichotomous key always has two contrasting statements at each step.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: A dichotomous key always has two contrasting statements at each step. [2]

items.stem: A student uses this dichotomous key to identify leaf-litter invertebrates. Key: 1a has legs ... go to 2; 1b has no legs ... go to 3 | 2a has six legs ... beetle; 2b does not have six legs ... woodlouse | 3a has a shell ... snail; 3b has no shell ... earthworm. The specimen has these features: has no shell; body is segmented; has no legs. Use the key to identify the specimen.
items.answer: earthworm
items.markingKey: earthworm: follow each pair of statements in turn [1]

items.stem: A student uses this dichotomous key to identify pond animals. Key: 1a body enclosed in a shell-like covering ... go to 2; 1b no shell-like covering ... go to 3 | 2a has jointed legs ... water flea; 2b has no jointed legs ... pond snail | 3a has jointed legs ... go to 4; 3b has no jointed legs ... leech | 4a has a tail or tail filaments ... damselfly nymph; 4b has no tail ... water boatman. The specimen has these features: has a tail or tail filaments; does not have three tail filaments; has jointed legs; no shell-like covering; tail ends in three flattened paddles. (a) Use the key to identify the specimen. (b) State the features that the key gives for the leech.
items.answer: (a) damselfly nymph (b) no shell-like covering; has no jointed legs
items.markingKey: (a) damselfly nymph [1] (b) features from the key: no shell-like covering; has no jointed legs [2]

items.stem: Daniel collects leaf-litter invertebrates on a field trip near Kathmandu. Their features are: snail: has no legs, has a shell, body is not segmented; millipede: has legs, does not have eight legs, does not have six legs, has two pairs of legs on most body segments; spider: has legs, has eight legs, has no wings; beetle: has legs, does not have eight legs, has six legs, has wings; slug: has no legs, has no shell, body is not segmented. (a) Construct a dichotomous key to identify these organisms. (b) Explain why the key must use features that do not change during the life of the organism or with the season.
items.answer: (a) 1a has legs ... go to 2; 1b has no legs ... go to 4 | 2a has eight legs ... spider; 2b does not have eight legs ... go to 3 | 3a has six legs ... beetle; 3b does not have six legs ... millipede | 4a has a shell ... snail; 4b has no shell ... slug (b) Otherwise the same species could be identified differently at different times (e.g. juveniles or seasonal changes).
items.markingKey: (a) paired contrasting statements at each step [1]; each organism reached at a separate end-point [1]; uses features given, not size or colour [1]; 4 steps [1] [4] (b) features must be constant [1]; reliable identification [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "arthropod"?
options: A hard external skeleton made of chitin that supports and protects an arthropod.
An invertebrate with jointed legs, a segmented body and an exoskeleton.
A flowering plant with one seed leaf, parallel leaf veins and flower parts in threes.
A plant with roots, stems and fronds that reproduces by spores, not seeds.
items.answer: An invertebrate with jointed legs, a segmented body and an exoskeleton.
items.markingKey: Arthropod: an invertebrate with jointed legs, a segmented body and an exoskeleton.

items.stem: Spiders and scorpions are arachnids, not insects. Give two features you could use to show this.
items.answer: They have four pairs of legs (not three) and a body in two parts with no antennae or wings.
items.markingKey: four pairs of legs [1]; two body parts / no antennae [1] [2]

items.stem: An organism found near Istanbul has these features: one pair of antennae; a body in three parts: head, thorax and abdomen. To which group does it belong?
items.answer: insects
items.markingKey: Insects: three pairs of jointed legs; a body in three parts: head, thorax and abdomen; one pair of antennae; two pairs of wings in most species.

items.stem: A plant found near Mumbai has these features: spores for reproduction; leaves called fronds. To which group does it belong?
items.answer: ferns
items.markingKey: Ferns: leaves called fronds; spores for reproduction; no flowers or seeds; roots, stems and leaves with xylem.

items.stem: Compare the features of a fern and a flowering plant.
items.answer: Both: plants with roots, stems, leaves, chlorophyll and xylem/phloem. Fern: fronds, spores in sporangia under fronds, no flowers, seeds or fruits. Flowering plant: flowers, seeds in ovaries forming fruits, monocots or dicots.
items.markingKey: two similarities [2]; three differences [3] [5]

items.stem: Jonas says: "Two species that look alike must be closely related." Explain whether Jonas is correct.
items.answer: Similar appearance can result from similar environments; DNA base sequences show relationships more reliably.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Similar appearance can result from similar environments; DNA base sequences show relationships more reliably. [2]

items.stem: A student in Hanoi states: "Mushrooms are plants because they grow in soil and do not move." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Mushrooms are fungi: they have no chlorophyll, cell walls of chitin and feed by extracellular digestion.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Mushrooms are fungi: they have no chlorophyll, cell walls of chitin and feed by extracellular digestion. [2]

items.stem: An organism has these features: single-celled; no nucleus: circular DNA in the cytoplasm. To which kingdom does it belong?
items.answer: prokaryotes
items.markingKey: Prokaryotes: single-celled; no nucleus: circular DNA in the cytoplasm; plasmids present; cell wall not made of cellulose; very small ribosomes.

items.stem: Part of the same gene was sequenced in four species. Species A: TTCATTTAACACGTAC; species C: TACATTTGATACATTT; species D: TTCATTTAACCCGTAC; species B: TTGATCTAACACTTAC. (a) Identify the species most closely related to A, showing your working. (b) Calculate the percentage of bases in species D that are the same as in species A.
items.answer: (a) Differences from A: C 6, D 1, B 3. Species D is most closely related. (b) 93.8%
items.markingKey: (a) counts differences correctly [1]; species D (fewest differences) [1] (b) (16 − 1) ÷ 16 × 100 = 93.8% [1] [3]

items.stem: Lina compares a 200-base section of DNA from three orchid species, X, Y and Z, found in different valleys near Hanoi. X and Y differ at 18 bases; X and Z differ at 23 bases; Y and Z differ at 22 bases. X and Z look very similar; Y looks different. (a) Calculate the percentage difference between the DNA of X and Z. (b) Suggest why X and Z look similar even though they are less closely related.
items.answer: (a) 11.5% (b) They live in similar habitats, so similar features were selected (convergence); appearance does not always show relationship.
items.markingKey: (a) 23 ÷ 200 × 100 [1] = 11.5% [1] [2] (b) similar environment / selection pressures [1]; visible features not reliable [1] [2]

items.stem: Which of these is an example of excretion?
options: Removal of faeces from the anus
Release of saliva into the mouth
Loss of hair from the scalp
Removal of carbon dioxide from the lungs
items.answer: Removal of carbon dioxide from the lungs
items.markingKey: CO₂ is a waste product of respiration (metabolism); faeces are egested, not excreted.

items.stem: Explain the difference between excretion and egestion.
items.answer: Excretion removes waste products of metabolism made inside cells (e.g. urea, CO₂); egestion removes undigested food (faeces) that was never absorbed into cells.
items.markingKey: excretion = metabolic waste [1]; egestion = undigested food that was never part of metabolism [1] [2]

items.stem: Hana grew bean seedlings in Kathmandu. A sample of seedlings had a fresh mass of 8.3 g and a dry mass of 0.8 g at the start. After 21 days a similar sample had a fresh mass of 13.2 g and a dry mass of 1.6 g. Calculate the percentage increase in dry mass.
Describe how a scientist could show that a sample of soil contains living organisms. Refer to at least three characteristics of living organisms in your answer.
items.answer: Use two samples, one sterilised by heating as a control. Measure carbon dioxide release / oxygen use (respiration) with hydrogencarbonate indicator; look for an increase in the number of organisms (reproduction / growth) on agar; test whether organisms take in nutrients (e.g. starch broken down); keep the conditions the same.
items.markingKey: control (heated soil) [1]; respiration test with indicator [1]; growth / reproduction evidence [1]; nutrition evidence [1]; fair test / conditions controlled [1] [5]

items.stem: A horse and a donkey can breed to produce a mule, which is infertile. What does this show?
options: Horses and donkeys are different species
Horses and donkeys are in different kingdoms
Horses and donkeys are the same species
items.answer: Horses and donkeys are different species
items.markingKey: Members of one species produce fertile offspring; mules are infertile hybrids.

items.stem: Lucas writes in a revision note: "A dichotomous key can use three choices at each step." Identify the error and write a correct statement.
items.answer: A dichotomous key always has two contrasting statements at each step.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: A dichotomous key always has two contrasting statements at each step. [2]

items.answer: A dichotomous key always has two contrasting statements at each step.

items.stem: A student uses this dichotomous key to identify pond animals. Key: 1a body enclosed in a shell-like covering ... water flea; 1b no shell-like covering ... go to 2 | 2a has jointed legs ... go to 3; 2b has no jointed legs ... flatworm | 3a has a tail or tail filaments ... mayfly nymph; 3b has no tail ... water boatman. The specimen has these features: has jointed legs; body enclosed in a shell-like covering; has no tail. Use the key to identify the specimen.
items.answer: water flea
items.markingKey: water flea: follow each pair of statements in turn [1]

items.stem: Three organisms have the scientific names Equus caballus, Vulpes vulpes and Equus zebra. (a) State which two are most closely related and give a reason. (b) State the genus of the third organism.
items.answer: (a) Equus caballus and Equus zebra: they share the genus Equus. (b) Vulpes
items.markingKey: (a) Equus caballus and Equus zebra [1]; same genus (Equus) [1] (b) Vulpes [1] [3]

items.stem: Noah collects leaves from trees in a park on a field trip near Cairo. Their features are: maple: leaf is a single blade, leaf edge has no spines, leaf edge has rounded or pointed lobes, lobes are pointed; ash: leaf is divided into leaflets, leaflets arranged in pairs along a central stalk; horse chestnut: leaf is divided into leaflets, leaflets spread out from one point; beech: leaf is a single blade, leaf edge has no spines, leaf edge has no lobes, leaf edge is smooth; holly: leaf is a single blade, leaf edge has spines. (a) Construct a dichotomous key to identify these organisms. (b) Explain why the key must use features that do not change during the life of the organism or with the season.
items.answer: (a) 1a leaf is divided into leaflets ... go to 2; 1b leaf is a single blade ... go to 3 | 2a leaflets spread out from one point ... horse chestnut; 2b leaflets arranged in pairs along a central stalk ... ash | 3a leaf edge has spines ... holly; 3b leaf edge has no spines ... go to 4 | 4a leaf edge has rounded or pointed lobes ... maple; 4b leaf edge has no lobes ... beech (b) Otherwise the same species could be identified differently at different times (e.g. juveniles or seasonal changes).
items.markingKey: (a) paired contrasting statements at each step [1]; each organism reached at a separate end-point [1]; uses features given, not size or colour [1]; 4 steps [1] [4] (b) features must be constant [1]; reliable identification [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "exoskeleton"?
options: A hard external skeleton made of chitin that supports and protects an arthropod.
A plant with roots, stems and fronds that reproduces by spores, not seeds.
A flowering plant with two seed leaves, branching leaf veins and flower parts in fours or fives.
A flowering plant with one seed leaf, parallel leaf veins and flower parts in threes.
items.answer: A hard external skeleton made of chitin that supports and protects an arthropod.
items.markingKey: Exoskeleton: a hard external skeleton made of chitin that supports and protects an arthropod.

items.stem: Lina says: "Whales and dolphins are fish because they live in water and have fins." Explain whether Lina is correct.
items.answer: They are mammals: they breathe air with lungs, have hair and feed their young on milk.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: They are mammals: they breathe air with lungs, have hair and feed their young on milk. [2]

items.stem: A plant found near Manila has these features: flower parts in multiples of four or five; leaves with branching (net) veins. To which group does it belong?
items.answer: dicotyledons
items.markingKey: Dicotyledons: two cotyledons in the seed; leaves with branching (net) veins; flower parts in multiples of four or five.

items.stem: A plant found near Singapore has these features: one cotyledon in the seed; leaves with parallel veins. To which group does it belong?
items.answer: monocotyledons
items.markingKey: Monocotyledons: one cotyledon in the seed; leaves with parallel veins; flower parts in multiples of three.

items.stem: Describe the features used to classify vertebrates into five groups.
items.answer: Skin covering (fur, feathers, dry scales, moist skin, wet scales), gas exchange (lungs/gills), eggs (shelled or not / live young), body temperature control, presence of mammary glands / external ears.
items.markingKey: one valid feature each for five groups [5]

items.stem: Isla says: "Viruses are the smallest type of bacteria." Explain whether Isla is correct.
items.answer: Viruses are not cells at all; bacteria are prokaryotic cells.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Viruses are not cells at all; bacteria are prokaryotic cells. [2]

items.stem: A student in Colombo states: "Two species that look alike must be closely related." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Similar appearance can result from similar environments; DNA base sequences show relationships more reliably.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Similar appearance can result from similar environments; DNA base sequences show relationships more reliably. [2]

items.stem: An organism has these features: cell walls made of chitin; no chlorophyll. To which kingdom does it belong?
items.answer: fungi
items.markingKey: Fungi: usually multicellular threads called hyphae (yeast is single-celled); cell walls made of chitin; no chlorophyll; feed by extracellular digestion (saprotrophic); store carbohydrate as glycogen.
